title: Fetch Data
jobContext: Every app you use — Instagram, Twitter, Amazon — fetches data from servers. When you load your feed, it's using fetch(). This is THE most important skill for building real web apps.

lesson.content: What You'll Learn
By the end of this lesson, you'll write a function that asks a server for a user's name and gets it back. Sounds simple — but this one skill is how ALL apps load data from the internet.
What is an API?

An **API** (Application Programming Interface) is a website that gives you data instead of a visual page. When you visit https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/1 in a browser, you see a block of text. That text is **JSON data** — structured information that computers can read. APIs are like restaurant kitchens: you place an order (a request), and the kitchen sends back your food (the data).
What is fetch()?

`fetch()` is a built-in JavaScript tool that asks a URL for data. Think of it like dialing a phone number: you give it an address (URL), and it calls that address to get information. `fetch()` always returns a **Promise** — a promise of data that will arrive later.
What is a Promise?

A **Promise** is exactly what it sounds like: a promise that something will happen in the future. When you order food at a restaurant, you get a receipt number (that's the Promise), and later your food arrives (that's the Promise resolving). Promises can be in three states: **pending** (waiting for food), **fulfilled** (food arrived), or **rejected** (kitchen burned down).
What is .then()?

`.then()` is how you say "when the data arrives, do this". It's like telling your friend: "When the pizza gets here, text me." You attach `.then()` to a Promise, and the code inside runs only after the Promise is fulfilled. `.then()` itself returns a Promise too, which is why you can chain them.
Let's break that down line by line:
`fetch('https://...')` — calls the server and returns a Promise. The request is sent, and JavaScript keeps running other code while waiting.
`.then(function(response) { ... })` — runs when the server responds. The `response` object contains the server's reply, but it's in a raw format we can't use yet.

`response.json()` — converts the raw response into a usable JavaScript object (an **object** is a collection of labeled data, like a file folder with labeled tabs). This also returns a Promise because converting takes time.
`.then(function(userData) { ... })` — runs with the converted data. `userData` is an object containing everything the API knows about user 1: name, email, address, phone, etc.
`return userData.name` — pulls just the `name` property out of the object (like opening the folder and taking only the tab labeled "name").
How do you build the URL?
The URL has two parts: a **base URL** that never changes, and an **id** that changes for each user. You combine them with `+`, the string concatenation operator (it glues text together).
Your Task

Write a function `getUser(id)` that fetches from `https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/` + the id, and returns a Promise that resolves to the user's **name**. For example, `getUser(1)` should eventually give you `"Leanne Graham"`.

The function should: (1) build the URL from the base + id, (2) call fetch() with that URL, (3) convert the response to JSON with `.then(res => res.json())`, (4) return just the name with `.then(data => data.name)`.

testCases.name: returns the correct user name for id 1

hints: Use fetch() + .then(res => res.json()) to get the data
Return data.name from the result — data is the user object, .name gets just their name

title: Promises & Await
jobContext: Modern codebases all use async/await. It's cleaner than .then() chains. If you're reading production code, this is what you'll see. Every line reads top-to-bottom like normal code.

lesson.content: What You'll Learn

In the last lesson, you used `.then()` to handle Promises. It works, but the code reads sideways instead of down. This lesson introduces `async` and `await` — two words that make Promise-based code read like normal step-by-step instructions.
What is async?

`async` is a keyword you put BEFORE a function: `async function name() { ... }`. It does two things: (1) it lets you use `await` inside the function, and (2) it automatically wraps the return value in a Promise. Even if you `return 5`, the caller gets a Promise that resolves to 5. Think of `async` as flipping a switch that tells JavaScript "this function deals with waiting."
What is await?

`await` means "pause right here and wait for this Promise to finish". It's like saying "wait for the toast to pop up before buttering it." `await` can ONLY be used inside `async` functions. While JavaScript is paused on an `await`, it can still handle other tasks — it doesn't freeze the whole program.
Side-by-Side Comparison
Here's the `.then()` version you already know, next to the `async/await` version. They do EXACTLY the same thing:

See the difference? The `async/await` version reads top-to-bottom, like a recipe. No sideways `.then()` nesting. Every line runs in order, and `await` just pauses at each step until the data is ready.

Why use async/await?

Three reasons: (1) **Readability** — code reads top-to-bottom like normal instructions, not nested sideways. (2) **Debugging** — stack traces show the actual line number that failed, not the middle of a `.then()` chain. (3) **Error handling** — you can use `try/catch` (next lesson) instead of `.catch()`. Every modern codebase prefers async/await.
Your Task

Write an `async function getPostTitle(id)` that fetches from `https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/` + the id and returns the post's title. Use `await` for both the `fetch()` call and the `.json()` conversion. Return `data.title`.

title: Handle Errors
jobContext: In real apps, APIs fail constantly — servers go down, networks cut out, users type wrong IDs. If you don't handle errors, your app crashes with ugly red screens. Error handling separates professional code from hobby projects.

lesson.content: What You'll Learn

So far you've written code that works when everything is perfect. But the real world is messy: servers crash, networks drop, users type invalid IDs. In this lesson, you'll learn to handle all of that gracefully so your app never crashes.
The Problem: APIs Fail

What happens with your current code when you call `getUser(99999)`? The server might return a **404** ("not found" status code). Or if there's a typo in the URL, JavaScript throws an error and your whole program stops. Users see nothing — or worse, a red error message.
What is try/catch?

`try/catch` is like a safety net for a tightrope walker. You put risky code inside `try { }`. If an error happens, instead of crashing, execution jumps to `catch (error) { }` where you handle it gracefully. Think of it as: "try this dangerous thing, and if it breaks, catch the pieces before they hit the ground."
The Surprising Thing About fetch()

Here's something that trips up beginners: **`fetch()` only throws an error for network problems** (like no internet connection or a typo in the domain name). If the server responds with a 404 ("user not found") or 500 ("server error"), `fetch()` considers that a SUCCESSFUL response — it got a reply, just not the one you wanted.
What is throw new Error()?

`throw` is how you manually create an error. `new Error('message')` creates an error object with a description. When you throw, execution immediately stops and jumps to the nearest `catch` block. You use it like this: `if (!response.ok) { throw new Error('User not found') }`.
Why return an error object instead of crashing?

When a function crashes, the user sees nothing — or a red error screen. When you return an error object like `{ error: true, message: '...' }`, the CALLER (the code that uses your function) can decide what to show the user: "User not found, please try a different ID." This is called **graceful error handling** — your app never explodes, it just reports what went wrong in a friendly way.
Your Task

Write an async function `safeGetUser(id)` that handles errors gracefully. On success, return the user data. On failure (network error, bad response, invalid ID), return `{ error: true, message: 'the error message' }`. Use `try/catch` and check `response.ok` before converting to JSON.

For the test cases: valid id (1) should return truthy data. Invalid id (9999) should return an error object. A bad id like -1 should also return an error object (the URL will fail to fetch because there's no user with id -1).

testCases.name: returns error object for invalid id

hints: Wrap your code in try { ... } catch (error) { ... }
After fetch(url), check if (!response.ok) and throw new Error('message')
Return { error: true, message: error.message } inside the catch block
